questions.prompt: Which list matches the inner-product axioms on a real vector space?
options: symmetry, linearity in the first argument, and \(\langle x,x \rangle > 0\) for \(x \ne 0\)
questions.explanation: A real inner product is symmetric, linear in each slot, and positive on nonzero vectors. Forcing every square to zero destroys positive definiteness. Skew-symmetry would make \(\\langle x,x \\rangle = 0\). Positivity alone does not give the angle formula.

questions.explanation: \(1\cdot 2 + 2\cdot 0 + 3\cdot(-1) = 2-3 = -1\). Dropping the last term leaves 2. Adding the absolute values gives 6, which is not the dot product.

questions.prompt: Two nonzero vectors are orthogonal when
questions.explanation: Orthogonality is \(\langle x, y \rangle = 0\). Equal length is a different condition, and the Cauchy-Schwarz equality case is about parallel vectors, not orthogonal ones. Integer coordinates say nothing about the angle.

questions.prompt: The Frobenius inner product sums the products of matching entries. For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), what is \(\langle A, B \rangle_F\)?
questions.explanation: The entrywise products are \(1, 0, 0, 3\), and they sum to 4. The same value is \(\mathrm{tr}(A^T B)\). Multiplying the determinants, \(3 \cdot 1 = 3\), is a different operation.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a 2 by 2 matrix</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">1   0</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">2   3</text></svg>

questions.prompt: The cosine of the angle between two nonzero vectors is
questions.explanation: The angle formula divides the inner product by the product of the lengths. The inner product alone still carries the lengths. The product of the lengths is the Cauchy-Schwarz upper bound, not the cosine. The length of the sum is the triangle inequality's subject.

questions.explanation: \(3\cdot 4 + 4\cdot 3 = 24\). Each vector has length 5, so the product of the lengths is 25, which is the Cauchy-Schwarz bound rather than the inner product. The difference of the coordinates would not produce 24.

questions.prompt: The Frobenius inner product of two real matrices of the same shape equals
options: the largest entry of either matrix
\(\mathrm{tr}(A^T B)\), the sum of the entrywise products
questions.explanation: Summing \(a_{ij} b_{ij}\) is the trace of \(A^T B\). Determinants and traces multiply different summaries of the two matrices. The largest entry ignores every other pair.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>symmetric 2 by 2 matrix</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">4   2</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">2   4</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 matrix with equal diagonal entries and equal off-diagonal entries.

questions.prompt: The 2-norm is the square root of the dot product of a vector with itself. What is \(\lVert(3,4)\rVert_2\)?
questions.explanation: \(\langle x,x \rangle = 9+16 = 25\), so the length is 5. The 1-norm is \(3+4 = 7\). Reporting 25 skips the square root.

questions.prompt: The pairing \(x_1 y_1 - x_2 y_2\) is not an inner product. What value does it give on the second standard basis vector with itself?
questions.explanation: The second term flips sign, so the pairing of \((0,1)\) with itself is \(-1\). An inner product would be positive. The ordinary dot product of that vector with itself is \(+1\), which is the sign this formula loses.

questions.prompt: Cauchy-Schwarz says \(\lvert(3,4)\cdot(4,3)\rvert\) cannot exceed the product of the lengths. What is that product of lengths?
questions.explanation: Each vector has length \(\sqrt{9+16} = 5\), so the product is 25. The inner product itself is 24, strictly below the bound, because the vectors are not parallel.

questions.prompt: Gram-Schmidt removes from a new vector the part parallel to the vectors already kept. That parallel part is a multiple of
options: the determinant of the two vectors
the sum \(u+v\), regardless of the inner product
a vector orthogonal to every later vector, chosen in advance
questions.explanation: The coefficient of \(u\) in \(v\) is the inner product \(\langle v, u \rangle\) divided by \(\langle u, u \rangle\). Subtracting that multiple leaves a vector orthogonal to \(u\). The determinant is an area, not the coefficient. Adding \(u\) and \(v\) does not cancel the parallel part.

questions.prompt: Directions \(d_i, d_j\) are conjugate for a symmetric positive definite \(Q\) when
options: \(Q\) is a multiple of the identity and nothing else is true
questions.explanation: Conjugacy is orthogonality in the inner product \(\langle u, v \rangle_Q = u^T Q v\). Ordinary orthogonality is the special case \(Q = I\). Opposite directions are linearly dependent, not conjugate, and a dot product of 1 is not the conjugacy condition.
